title: Smallholding bookkeeping basics
subtitle: What records a smallholding needs to keep, why they matter, and a simple system for keeping them.
excerpt: Most smallholders start keeping records because HMRC or a grant scheme requires it. The ones who benefit most from their records go further: they track which enterprises make a surplus and which do not, whether any livestock batch was profitable, and what the actual cost per kilogram of home-produced meat or eggs was. A simple spreadsheet with a few minutes of entries per week builds into a useful picture within a year.
sourceNotes: HMRC, Self Assessment guide for the self-employed (2023/24). Defra, Agricultural record-keeping requirements (2023). NFU, Farm business record guidance (2022). Graham Boyes and Andrew Dilnot, The DIY Investor (2022), chapter on basic business records. SAC Consulting, Smallholder enterprise costing guide (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: A record of income and expenditure assigned to a specific enterprise on the holding (e.g., pigs, poultry, market garden). Separating enterprises shows which ones pay their way and which are subsidised by others.

A running record of when money comes in and goes out of the holding, rather than when the corresponding purchase or sale was made. A cash flow view helps avoid the situation of being technically profitable on paper but unable to pay a bill due next week.

content.text: Any smallholding that sells produce, receives farm payments, or claims business expenses against income needs to keep records. In the UK, this means filing a self-assessment return if turnover exceeds the registration threshold or if the activity is considered trading by HMRC. But even below that threshold, records are useful: you cannot improve what you cannot measure.
The minimum you need
A record of every purchase: date, supplier, what it was, the amount.
A record of every sale: date, buyer, what was sold, the amount.
Receipts or invoices for every purchase: HMRC requires these to support any expense claim.
Enterprise accounts
The next step beyond a single income-and-expenditure record is separating the holding into
enterprise accounts

: one column for pigs, one for poultry, one for market garden. Shared costs such as machinery and utilities are split between enterprises in proportion. This shows which enterprises pay their way and which are running at a loss.
Cash flow
A simple
cash flow statement

records when money actually moves. The feed bill arrives in March and is paid in April, so it appears in April's cash flow even if it belongs to March's enterprise account. Tracking both avoids the trap of knowing the enterprise makes a surplus but being unable to pay a bill when it falls due.
A simple spreadsheet structure

One sheet per calendar year. Columns: date, description, category (feed / vet / equipment / sales / labour / grant), enterprise (pigs / poultry / garden / general), income, expenditure, running balance. Filter by enterprise at year end to get the enterprise accounts. Filter by month to get a cash flow picture.
What else to record
Animal movement records: required by law for cattle, pigs, sheep, and goats. Kept in the holding register.
Medicine records: required by law for any prescription or POM-VPS product administered to food-producing animals. Record product, batch number, dose, date, animal, and withdrawal period.
Spraying and fertiliser records if you manage land that receives farm payments under an agri-environment scheme.

A smallholding that has not yet been profitable is not automatically a business in HMRC's view: HMRC may class it as a hobby if there is no reasonable expectation of profit. This distinction affects what expenses can be set against other income. A clear set of records showing costs, income, and a plan toward profitability strengthens the case for business status.
